title: Example 19-3: Morse Code with Word Sounds

illustrates.quote: Follow print when sounds such as dit, di, and dah represent the Morse code sounds. a. Use a hyphen to connect the sounds of a single letter. b. Use a space to separate the letters within words. c. Follow print for punctuation. d. Line breaks are between words. Do not divide words between braille lines.

blocks.text: dah-dah dah-dah-dah di-dah-dit di-di-dit dit, dah-di-dah-dit dah-dah-dah dah-di-dit dit.
blocks.features: Braille shows this flush (zero indent), so built blocked:true.

print.notes: Plain prose paragraph (Morse sounds spelled out as words) with ordinary comma/period punctuation — 19.4.2's own point is that this needs no special handling at all, unlike 19.4.1's dot/dash symbol form.

braille.notes: Byte-identical between run A and run B, and independently re-derived from source-lines 15098-15100. Forward-translating the print paragraph above through Emboss's own translator (uebG2) reproduces this braille exactly, byte-for-byte, confirming both the wording and that 19.4.2's hyphen/comma/period all need no special handling.

resolution: Braille unchanged (A and B agree; independently re-derived and forward-translation-verified). Print side: both runs agreed on the wording; adopted B's single flowing block (A's internal line break was an arbitrary transcription artifact, not something in the source — Emboss wraps the one paragraph itself).
